details:
I don't really know the *ideal* way to implement this - but some way to leave evidence of the last user + avatar ID rendered on disk post-exit would be useful.

Below is a potential way this could be implemented, that could potentially be both simple and performant enough on desktop to actually be feasible, while being open enough to allow for future use cases:

Open a memory-mapped file in a supervisor process. This process exists to hold the handle open, even beyond the actual game's exit, as on Windows closing the handle will result in the file being immediately deleted. This should ideally be fully isolated, without even a parent/child relationship, so a GPU hang or crash does not result in early termination.

This handle (whether a file path, an anonymous file handle, etc) is then passed to VRC as a launch argument. This handle has the current user + avatar ID written to it every time a render starts, and erased once a render finished. Maybe a u32 at the start that defines the length of the data, being set to 0 post-render. Either way, as this is memory-mapped, the overhead here is basically 0 as it doesn't require any syscalls to touch - it's just managed as a standard fixed sized array.

When the main VRChat process is closed for any reason, regardless of exit code, the file (via the retained handle) is read by the supervisor process. If the handle shows that the file was not flushed with a 0 at the start (or empty, or what have you) this can signal a crash, and leave evidence on-disk as a real file to then auto-report next startup, or logged, or even auto-uploaded by said supervisor process. This way an avatar (or otherwise) crasher can be detected as a result of either a large number of sudden reports (entire lobby crashes) or repeated crashes from a single user, or multiple separate reports of a single avatar ID, etc.

As memory-mapped I/O on Windows is very fast and runs little to no risk of wearing out your disk (due to aggressive OS-side caching), this feels like a fairly reasonable solution - even in large lobbies. The supervisor process could also upload these crash reports automatically, though I would also like, as a user, to have a way to go back and inspect these regardless of crash log - this way I can moderate event instances more effectively. Basically creating a sacrificial canary client that catches lobby crashers so I can boot them out of lobbies and group ban them.

On Linux, this can be slower if the file is backed by a real disk, but writing to a file within /dev/shm is an easy way to avoid this. As only creating the initial mapping is expensive, this is pretty fast - and on linux you can enforce direct i/o here to bypass the page cache, which for a memfs-backed file (i.e. one in /dev/shm) will usually result in even lower overhead.

This can also be used to detect other user-specific or avatar-specific crash events, such as when processing animators and other such systems. Though this would depend on how these systems are executed, and like everything else this would need to be measured.

If providing the avatar ID here is an issue - as any unprivileged user could theoretically read this - a user ID + timestamp could be recorded, and the avatar used at the time could be correlated server-side. For the extra moderation use case, a user ID is more than enough for someone to develop an external moderation warning tool with (though this could easily be baked into the standard client too!)

Worth a note here: windows immediately removes the file when no handles are held. Other platforms may keep it around. So ideally the file created/opened should have a unique name or handle per instance of VRC. It would also be ideal to have a file/handle per supervisor PID to ensure that multiple clients running at once (club bots, testing, etc) don't cause problems with eachother.

On Windows, this would be opening a file with FILE_ATTRIBUTE_TEMPORARY | FILE_FLAG_DELETE_ON_CLOSE

On Linux, this would be opening a file in /dev/shm with the attribute of TMPFILE set. This attribute does not exist on OSX I believe, but there are likely other routes. Same with mobile platforms.
title: Some way to detect the last rendering avatar prior to a game crash
